references.text: Caring for the foreigner, the widow, and the fatherless is a recurring theme in the Mosaic Law. Here in Exodus, the Israelites are warned against oppressing foreigners and widows.
The command not to oppress the foreigner is repeated, with reference to Israel's own experience as foreigners in Egypt.
Leviticus gives the same command to treat the foreigner as a native-born and love them as yourself.
The Lord himself is described as one who defends the cause of the fatherless and the widow, and loves the foreigner.
A curse is pronounced on anyone who perverts justice for the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.
Isaiah urges people to seek justice, help the oppressed, defend the fatherless, and plead the case of the widow.
Jeremiah warns against oppressing the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.
The word of the Lord through Jeremiah commands doing what is right and just, and rescuing the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor.
Ezekiel accuses Jerusalem of having wronged the fatherless and the widow.
Zechariah conveys the Lord's word not to oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner, or the poor.
Malachi warns against those who oppress the hired worker, the widow, and the fatherless, and who pervert justice for the foreigner.
James defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in their distress.
